# Cellarity Announces Close of $121 Million Series C Financing

| Section Heading | Section Content |
| --- | --- |
| Overview | SOMERVILLE, Mass., October 4, 2022 – Cellarity, a life sciences company founded by Flagship Pioneering to transform the way medicines are created, announced today the completion of a $121 million Series C financing, bringing its total funding raised to date to $274 million. In addition to participation by Flagship Pioneering and other Series B investors, four new investors participated, including Kyowa Kirin Co. Ltd. and Hanwha Impact Partners. The proceeds of the financing will be used to grow Cellarity’s talent base, strengthen its platform, and advance its pipeline toward the clinic.  “We welcome our new investors and appreciate the continued support of our current investors,” said Fabrice Chouraqui, PharmD, CEO of Cellarity and a CEO-Partner at Flagship Pioneering. “By shifting the focus from a single target to the underlying cellular dysfunction, our platform unravels the complexity of disease biology to create medicines never before possible. We have already made significant progress in confirming the unique capability of our platform with the development of compounds that have been validated in vitro and in vivo, including in higher species. With this financing, we plan to advance our pipeline and showcase the immense possibilities of our approach.”  To create medicines, Cellarity looks beyond individual molecular targets and instead focuses on the whole cell. The company uses single-cell technologies to identify cellular drivers during the transition from health to disease and applies proprietary deep learning models to create drugs that reverse disease at the level of the cell. Cellarity has developed unique capabilities to link biology and chemistry with high dimensional, transcriptomic data to design medicines against the cellular signature of the disease. The Cellarity platform provides critical insights into cellular dysfunction and reveals new biology through which we can address a range of diseases, including those which presently lack a known druggable target.  “Cellarity is truly rewriting the rules of drug creation. Disease isn’t driven by one mechanism or protein, so Cellarity has developed the ability to solve disease through the lens of the entire cell,” said Stephen Berenson, Chairperson of Cellarity’s Board of Directors and Managing Partner at Flagship Pioneering. “Since the cell is a fuller representation of disease, the platform is uniquely designed to drive higher translatability and clinical success, creating important new medicines for internal pipeline development as well as with partners.” |
| About Cellarity | Cellarity’s mission is to fundamentally redesign the way drugs are created. By shifting the focus from a single target to understanding the whole cell, Cellarity unravels complex disease biology to create treatments never before possible. Founded by Flagship Pioneering in 2017, Cellarity has developed unique capabilities combining high-resolution data, single-cell technologies, and machine learning to unravel complex disease biology and purposefully design breakthrough medicines. As Cellarity’s medicines are created against many drivers of cellular disease instead of a single target, their approach is designed to drive higher clinical translatability and success and is applicable to a vast array of disease areas. The company currently has programs ongoing in several disease areas including those in metabolic disease, hematology, and immuno-oncology. |
| About Flagship Pioneering | Flagship Pioneering conceives, creates, resources, and develops first-in-category bioplatform companies to transform human health and sustainability. Since its launch in 2000, the firm has, through its Flagship Labs unit, applied its unique hypothesis-driven innovation process to originate and foster more than 100 scientific ventures, resulting in more than $100 billion in aggregate value. To date, Flagship has deployed over $2.9 billion in capital toward the founding and growth of its pioneering companies alongside more than $19 billion of follow-on investments from other institutions. The current Flagship ecosystem comprises 41 transformative companies, including Denali Therapeutics (NASDAQ: DNLI), Evelo Biosciences (NASDAQ: EVLO), Foghorn Therapeutics (NASDAQ: FHTX), Moderna (NASDAQ: MRNA), Omega Therapeutics (NASDAQ: OMGA), Rubius Therapeutics (NASDAQ: RUBY), Sana Biotechnology (NASDAQ: SANA), and Seres Therapeutics (NASDAQ: MCRB). ### AdvanCell Successfully Completes an Oversubscribed US$112M Series C Financing

**Sydney, Australia – 3 February 2025** – AdvanCell, a clinical-stage radiopharmaceutical company developing innovative cancer therapeutics, today announced the successful completion of an oversubscribed US$112 million Series C financing. This milestone funding round was co-led by **SV Health Investors**, **Sanofi Ventures**, **Abingworth,** and **SymBiosis**. Additional support came from existing investor **Morningside**, alongside new investors **Tenmile**, **Brandon Capital**, and others.

Since its founding in June 2019, AdvanCell has grown from a belief in the potential of Targeted Alpha Therapy into a global organisation with 60 passionate team members, a 40,000-square- foot manufacturing facility, world-class pre-clinical infrastructure, a potentially best-in-class drug for prostate cancer that is in trials, and a deep and developing pipeline of assets.

This investment will fuel AdvanCell’s ongoing efforts to expand its manufacturing capacity, accelerate the clinical development of its pipeline of radionuclide therapies, and advance its mission of delivering life-changing treatments to cancer patients worldwide.

AdvanCell is currently enrolling patients for the highest dose cohort of its multi-center TheraPb Ph I/II dose escalation clinical trial of ADVC001 for metastatic prostate cancer, a potentially best-in-class Targeted Alpha Therapy. The trial aims to demonstrate the safety and efficacy of Pb-212-based radionuclide treatment.

As part of the financing, **Jamil M. Beg** from SV Health Investors, **Christopher Gagliardi** from Sanofi Ventures, and **Bali Muralidhar** from Abingworth have joined the AdvanCell Board of Directors. They bring extensive industry expertise to support the company’s growth and join existing directors **Bill Ferris AC**, **Anthony Aiudi**, **Kevin Cameron**, and **Andrew Adamovich**.

**Jamil M. Beg**, Partner at SV Health Investors, commented:

“We are delighted to support AdvanCell’s growth and play a role in its remarkable journey through leading this oversubscribed Series C. We have looked long and deep at the field of radionuclide therapies and are confident that AdvanCell stands out with a first-in-class Pb-212- PSMA program and a best-in-class manufacturing platform. The company’s exceptional team, technologies, robust infrastructure, collaborations with some of the world’s largest pharma companies and ability to consistently execute, position it to truly change outcomes for patients. We are excited to help AdvanCell realize its potential in transforming cancer care globally.”

AdvanCell was founded on the belief that Targeted Alpha Therapies could change the course of cancer treatment and that the scalable supply of isotopes would enable the development of multiple practice-changing drugs. Radionuclide therapies for prostate cancer and gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumours have transformed patient care. Pb-212 Targeted Alpha Therapy has the potential to further advance this progress by leveraging the radiobiological and physical attributes of Pb-212 to make life-changing treatments for patients.

“This successful Series C round demonstrates strong confidence in our vision and capabilities,” said **Andrew Adamovich**, CEO of AdvanCell. “We are grateful for the continued support from our existing investors, particularly the long-term support from Morningside and are excited to welcome new partners who share our commitment to transforming cancer care.

With this funding, AdvanCell is well-positioned to scale our manufacturing operations and progress our cutting-edge therapies towards commercialization.”

The Series C funding represents a significant step in AdvanCell’s journey to become a global leader in radionuclide-based cancer therapeutics.

**About SV Health Investors**

SV Health Investors is a leading healthcare fund manager committed to investing in tomorrow’s healthcare breakthroughs. With approximately $2bn in assets under management and a truly transatlantic presence with offices in Boston and London, SV has built an extensive network of talented investment professionals and experienced industry veterans. Since its founding in 1993, SV has invested in, created and built more than 200 companies attracting global talent, entrepreneurs and pharma partners. To date, these investments have resulted in the licensing of 26 novel drugs and six new drug classes able to treat indications with unmet medical needs and deliver positive impact to patients. **About Sanofi Ventures**

**About Abingworth**

Abingworth is a leading transatlantic life sciences investment firm and part of the global investment firm Carlyle (NASDAQ: CG). Abingworth helps transform cutting-edge science into novel medicines by providing capital and expertise to top calibre management teams building world-class companies. Since 1973, Abingworth has invested in over 185 life science companies, leading to 50+ M&As and more than 75 IPOs. Our therapeutic focused investments fall into three categories: seed and early-stage, development stage, and clinical co- development. Abingworth supports its portfolio companies with a team of experienced professionals at offices in London, Menlo Park (California), and Boston. For more information, please visit www.abingworth.com.

# What are the top cell therapy startups by total funding raised?

## SUMMARY

Iovance Biotherapeutics has raised the most equity funding in cell therapy, at roughly $3.1 billion, ahead of Legend Biotech at about $2.4 billion, Sana Biotechnology at at least $1.7 billion and Immatics at roughly $1.4 billion.

The funding leaderboard is unusually top-heavy. The first five companies account for roughly $9.7 billion, while the top 20 reach about $21.6 billion in cumulative equity financing.

These totals do not look like a conventional venture-capital ranking. Most of the companies near the top have been public for years, so IPOs, follow-on offerings, PIPEs and ATM sales now account for a large share of lifetime funding.

Private companies can still raise enormous rounds. Arsenal Biosciences has accumulated roughly $630 million, including a $325 million Series C, while OriCell, Sonoma, Umoja, AvenCell and Aspen have each attracted hundreds of millions without building the decade-long public financing histories of Iovance or Legend.

Recent capital is spreading beyond the oncology programs that dominate the historical ranking. Autoimmune CAR-T, in-vivo cell engineering, regenerative medicine and next-generation TIL approaches are all attracting nine-figure financings or major pharmaceutical transactions.

In-vivo CAR-T is one of the sharper shifts. Umoja raised $100 million, while pharmaceutical buyers have paid heavily for Capstan and EsoBiotec, showing that direct programming of immune cells inside the body has moved into serious strategic territory.

Solid tumors remain expensive and risky, but investors have not walked away. Arsenal, Obsidian, Immatics and OriCell have all raised large amounts around differentiated approaches to T-cell targeting, TIL engineering or solid-tumor CAR-T.

Manufacturing is almost a funding category of its own. Cell therapy companies are raising money not only for clinical programs but also for automation, internal manufacturing, logistics and technologies that could eliminate parts of the ex-vivo production chain.

Large cumulative funding is not a reliable proxy for success. Adaptimmune, Achilles, Gamida Cell and Instil Bio all raised substantial amounts before restructuring, selling assets, winding down or sharply changing strategy.

At the same time, relatively lightly funded companies can generate enormous strategic value. EsoBiotec reached a potential $1 billion acquisition despite little disclosed venture funding, while Arcellx's reconstructed fundraising was tiny beside the roughly $7.8 billion implied equity value cited around its Gilead acquisition.

The current market is still capable of producing very large checks, but they are more concentrated. Investors increasingly want a defined clinical program, unusual manufacturing advantage, convincing human data or a clear answer to a problem that earlier cell therapies failed to solve.

## How far ahead is Iovance Biotherapeutics in cell therapy funding?

Iovance is clearly number one by cumulative equity raised in our ranking, with roughly $700 million more funding than second-place Legend Biotech.

The gap comes from years of repeated public-market fundraising rather than one giant venture round. Iovance has financed the development, manufacturing and commercial launch of its TIL platform through numerous stock offerings and ATM programs.

The company was also the first in this ranking to turn a TIL program into an FDA-approved commercial product. The FDA granted accelerated approval to Amtagvi, Iovance's lifileucel, for previously treated advanced melanoma in 2024. That required building manufacturing capacity and funding a commercial organization on top of the usual clinical-development costs.

Iovance was still raising equity recently. Its SEC filing for the second quarter of 2026 shows $49.6 million of net proceeds during that quarter through its ATM program. The filing also says the company had a facility allowing it to sell up to $350 million of common stock over time.

So Iovance's $3.1 billion total is the cumulative financing history of a company that has gone all the way from development-stage biotech to commercial cell-therapy manufacturer. That is a very different funding story from a private Series B company raising money to reach its first clinical readout.

## Is Legend Biotech catching Iovance in total funding?

Legend Biotech is the closest challenger to Iovance, and it is still adding substantial amounts of equity capital.

Legend ranks second in our reconstruction at around $2.4 billion. Its latest major financing was an underwritten public offering announced in June 2026. The company priced 7.7 million American Depositary Shares at $29.35 each, for expected gross proceeds of about $226 million before any exercise of the underwriters' option.

Legend is no longer an early cell-therapy developer. Its BCMA CAR-T therapy Carvykti, developed with Johnson & Johnson, is already FDA-approved for multiple myeloma. Funding therefore supports a company with an approved product, international development programs and continuing manufacturing requirements.

The roughly $700 million gap with Iovance remains substantial, but Legend is close enough that the top two form a separate tier from most of the ranking. Sana, in third place, trails Legend by roughly another $700 million.

## Why has Sana Biotechnology raised so much money?

Sana reached the top three because investors funded an unusually broad cell-engineering platform very aggressively before the company had mature clinical data.

Sana's 2021 IPO alone raised $587.5 million before the underwriters' option, one of the largest biotech IPOs of that cycle. That came after very large private financings, pushing the company's reconstructed cumulative equity funding above $1.7 billion.

The company has continued tapping public markets. Sana reported $47.4 million of gross proceeds through its ATM program during 2025, alongside an $86.3 million underwritten offering.

Sana is also a useful warning against reading funding totals as a simple success ranking. Its work across engineered cells, hypoimmune technology and multiple disease areas gives it more possible upside, but it also demands more capital.

The $1.7 billion figure tells us that Sana persuaded investors to finance a very large technical vision. It does not tell us that the company has already converted that spending into equivalent commercial value.

## Why are so many of the most funded cell therapy companies already public?

Cell therapy development burns so much capital that the largest companies usually cannot remain dependent on venture rounds for long.

Of the top 20 companies in our ranking, most have already reached public markets at some point. IPO proceeds are only the beginning. Once listed, companies can return repeatedly through follow-on offerings, registered directs, PIPEs and ATM programs.

Nkarta illustrates the size of those later financings. It raised roughly $240 million in a single underwritten public offering in March 2024. Legend added approximately $226 million in its 2026 offering. Century Therapeutics raised $135 million privately from institutional investors despite already being listed. Kyverna added roughly $105 million in gross proceeds from its late-2025 follow-on transaction.

Those deals can be as large as, or larger than, private biotech Series B and Series C rounds. Over several years they push cumulative funding totals far above what a normal venture-funding database might suggest when someone thinks only in terms of pre-IPO rounds.

This is where "startup funding" gets fuzzy in cell therapy. The underlying businesses can remain clinical-stage biotechnology companies for years after listing, and they continue consuming development capital in much the same way a private startup does.

## Which cell therapy companies have raised big rounds most recently?

The market is still producing nine-figure cell therapy financings, but investors are choosing their bets much more selectively than during the broad biotech boom.

Immatics raised $150 million through an underwritten offering in August 2026. The final amount differs from the earlier $173 million figure in our working dataset, so we use the company's announced $150 million gross offering figure for the latest round.

Obsidian closed its $350 million private placement shortly before that, alongside the completion of its transaction with Galera. Century Therapeutics raised $135 million in January 2026. Legend priced a roughly $226 million offering in June. OriCell completed more than $110 million of pre-IPO financing in April.

Kyverna raised roughly $105 million in gross proceeds from its late-2025 follow-on, while Aspen Neuroscience closed a $115 million Series C around the same period.

That is already a substantial cluster of nine-figure financings. Cell therapy has not become an unfundable category. Capital is still there when investors see a program, platform or clinical trajectory worth concentrating money behind.

## Is cell therapy funding moving from cancer into autoimmune disease?

Yes, autoimmune cell therapy has become one of the clearest destinations for new capital, even though oncology still dominates cumulative funding.

The historical ranking is heavily shaped by cancer. Iovance, Legend, Immatics, Kite, Lyell, Atara, Adaptimmune, Instil, Caribou, CARsgen, Obsidian, Arsenal, TScan and several other highly funded companies were built primarily around oncology.

Newer financing tells a broader story. Kyverna is centered on CAR-T for autoimmune diseases and raised about $105 million in its latest follow-on. Century's $135 million 2026 placement supports a portfolio that now includes type 1 diabetes and autoimmune programs. Nkarta has been developing NKX019 in autoimmune disease. AvenCell explicitly describes autoimmune disease as part of the potential reach of its switchable CAR-T platform.

The biggest strategic clue may be acquisition activity. AstraZeneca acquired Gracell partly for opportunities spanning oncology and autoimmune disease, while AbbVie's agreement to pay up to $2.1 billion for Capstan Therapeutics centered on an in-vivo CAR-T approach being developed for autoimmune conditions.

The money accumulated over the last decade still looks predominantly like cancer funding. The marginal dollar being deployed today is much more willing to chase immune reset outside oncology.

## Is in-vivo CAR-T becoming a serious funding category?

In-vivo CAR-T has moved well beyond the "interesting experiment" stage and is now attracting both major venture rounds and billion-dollar pharmaceutical deals.

Umoja Biopharma raised $100 million in a 2025 Series C specifically to push its in-vivo CAR-T pipeline through clinical milestones. Capstan Therapeutics had raised about $340 million in our dataset before AbbVie agreed to acquire it for up to $2.1 billion in cash.

EsoBiotec provides another strong example. Its disclosed venture funding was small relative to the leaders in our ranking, yet AstraZeneca bought the company in 2025 for $425 million upfront and up to $575 million in additional payments. AstraZeneca highlighted the possibility of engineering immune cells directly inside the patient rather than extracting, modifying and reinfusing them.

Kelonia Therapeutics, another in-vivo cell-engineering company, was also acquired after raising about $50 million according to our reconstruction.

The attraction is pretty clear. Conventional autologous CAR-T can require complex collection, manufacturing, logistics and conditioning. An in-vivo system that reliably programs immune cells inside the body could remove several expensive steps at once.

We still do not know which technical approach will ultimately work best at commercial scale. What has changed is the amount of serious money willing to find out.

## Are investors still funding cell therapies for solid tumors?

Solid-tumor cell therapy remains one of the best-funded high-risk bets in biotechnology.

Arsenal Biosciences raised $325 million to advance programmable T-cell therapies for solid tumors. Obsidian secured $350 million around its public-market transaction to develop engineered TIL therapies, including programs in melanoma and non-small-cell lung cancer. Immatics raised another $150 million while developing a PRAME franchise that includes TCR-T cell therapy across multiple solid tumors.

OriCell's latest financing adds another example. The company raised more than $110 million ahead of a planned capital-market step while advancing CAR-T programs for solid tumors, including hepatocellular carcinoma.

These companies are attacking the same broad problem from different directions: better T-cell targeting, TIL engineering, logic gating, intracellular cancer targets and more controllable cell behavior.

Investors have already watched many solid-tumor cell therapy programs disappoint. Yet the money going into Arsenal, Obsidian, Immatics and OriCell shows the category itself has not been abandoned. Capital has moved toward companies that can explain why their version should behave differently from earlier attempts.

## Are allogeneic "off-the-shelf" cell therapies still attracting money?

Allogeneic cell therapy is still well funded, although investors no longer appear willing to finance the idea simply because it promises an off-the-shelf product.

Century Therapeutics, Caribou Biosciences, Nkarta, Adicet Bio, AvenCell and several other highly funded companies are developing allogeneic or donor-derived approaches. Roche's acquisition of Poseida also brought donor-derived CAR-T programs into a major pharmaceutical company.

The logic remains compelling. Making cells in advance could shorten treatment time, standardize manufacturing and potentially spread fixed production costs across more doses.

But years of clinical development have made the questions tougher. The cells must persist, avoid immune rejection, remain potent and deliver enough efficacy to compete with autologous products that already work very well in several blood cancers.

That explains the current funding pattern. Investors still write large checks, as Century's $135 million placement shows, but increasingly want a differentiated biological answer rather than the generic promise of cheaper manufacturing.

## Is autologous cell therapy losing investor support?

Autologous cell therapy is still attracting huge amounts of capital, especially when investors see strong efficacy or a credible route into solid tumors.

Iovance is the most funded company in the entire ranking and sells an autologous TIL therapy. Legend's Carvykti is an autologous CAR-T. Obsidian raised $350 million around an engineered autologous TIL program. Arsenal's programs also involve highly engineered patient-specific T cells.

Aspen Neuroscience provides a completely different example outside cancer. Its $115 million Series C backs an autologous iPSC-derived neuronal replacement therapy for Parkinson's disease.

The manufacturing burden has not killed the model. Investors will tolerate a complicated process when the therapy may deliver an outcome that simpler medicines cannot.

The pressure is coming from another direction: autologous approaches increasingly have to prove that the clinical benefit is worth the logistics. The arrival of in-vivo and better allogeneic systems raises that bar, but it has not made patient-specific cell therapy obsolete.

## Are TIL therapies becoming a real investment category?

TIL therapy has gained much more financial credibility since Iovance turned the modality into an approved product.

Iovance's Amtagvi became the first FDA-approved tumor-derived T-cell therapy for advanced melanoma in 2024. That commercial milestone changed the discussion for every company trying to improve the TIL model because the modality is no longer purely experimental.

Obsidian is the clearest next-generation financing example. Its $350 million private placement supports amsoki-cel, formerly OBX-115, an engineered TIL therapy designed to provide regulated IL-15 activity. The combined company began trading on Nasdaq under the OBX ticker after its transaction with Galera.

Instil Bio also raised very large amounts around autologous TIL development, although its subsequent strategic changes show how unforgiving the field can be.

The financing story today is less about whether TIL can work at all. Iovance answered part of that question. The harder investment question is whether engineered TIL products can improve efficacy, manufacturing or patient experience enough to justify another generation of spending.

## Why are investors putting so much money into cell therapy manufacturing?

Manufacturing can decide whether a promising cell therapy becomes a scalable medicine, so investors are effectively funding factories, logistics and process development alongside the science.

This is especially obvious in autologous therapy. Cells have to move from a patient to a manufacturing system and back again, often under tight time constraints. Each additional manipulation step creates cost and operational risk.

That helps explain why different financing themes keep converging on manufacturing. Nkarta said its $240 million offering would partly fund internal manufacturing capabilities. Aspen talks about automation and robotics as part of making personalized cell therapy commercially viable. In-vivo companies such as Umoja and the acquired EsoBiotec are trying to remove much of the ex-vivo manufacturing chain altogether.

Process engineering can be almost as strategically important as the biological target in this market. A better receptor is valuable; a better way to manufacture, or avoid manufacturing, the therapy can change the economics of the whole product.

## Who are the biggest investors backing cell therapy startups?

A relatively small group of specialist biotech investors keeps appearing across major cell therapy financings.

RA Capital appears across companies including Century Therapeutics, Nkarta and Obsidian. TCGX led Century's $135 million placement and Vor Bio's $75 million financing and also appears among Obsidian's existing investors. ARCH Venture Partners is prominent in Arsenal Biosciences and Aspen Neuroscience.

Cormorant, OrbiMed, Foresite, Deep Track, RTW and Samsara BioCapital also recur across the market. Strategic investors add another layer: Regeneron Ventures backed Arsenal, Bristol Myers Squibb has appeared in several cell-therapy syndicates, Bayer helped create BlueRock, and major pharmaceutical companies have repeatedly bought entire platforms.

The overlap is useful because these are not generalist investors wandering into one fashionable round. Many have financed cell therapy repeatedly across different modalities, diseases and development stages.

They are not all betting on the same technology either. The same sophisticated capital base is spread across autologous, allogeneic, TIL, NK, Treg, iPSC and in-vivo approaches.

## Does a huge funding total mean a cell therapy company is succeeding?

No. Cell therapy has several examples where enormous cumulative funding was followed by restructuring, asset sales, shutdowns or disappointing shareholder outcomes.

Adaptimmune raised roughly $813 million of equity in our reconstruction and became one of the best-funded engineered T-cell companies in the field. Yet in 2025 it agreed to sell Tecelra and several other cell-therapy assets to US WorldMeds for $55 million upfront plus possible milestone payments, and it subsequently delisted from Nasdaq.

Achilles Therapeutics raised roughly $403 million before winding down. Gamida Cell raised at least roughly $432 million before its public-company story ended in an acquisition following severe financial pressure.

Instil Bio raised about $749 million, including a roughly $368 million IPO, but later radically reduced its original TIL ambitions.

Cumulative funding is useful as a measure of how much capital investors committed, not as a proxy for value creation. In cell therapy, a company can spend several hundred million dollars simply discovering that a biological or manufacturing problem is harder than expected.

## How much of cell therapy funding is concentrated in the biggest companies?

Cell therapy funding is highly concentrated: the top 20 companies in our dataset have raised about $21.6 billion of equity between them.

The top five alone account for roughly $9.7 billion. The first ten reach about $14.6 billion.

That concentration is partly mechanical. Once a company reaches public markets, every subsequent offering adds to its lifetime total. A long-lived public biotech can therefore accumulate more equity than a younger private company even when the younger company is raising much larger rounds today.

Still, the difference is striking. Many companies in the lower half of the ranking have raised less than $50 million, while Iovance alone is around $3.1 billion.

The market effectively contains two financing worlds: a small set of mature developers with access to repeated nine-figure transactions, and a much larger group that has to reach meaningful scientific milestones with tens rather than hundreds of millions.

## Are cell therapy acquisitions validating the money investors put into the sector?

Several acquisitions show that pharmaceutical companies will pay far more than the capital originally invested when they want a specific cell-therapy asset or platform.

Gilead's $11.9 billion acquisition of Kite remains the clearest historical example. Kite had raised roughly $1.1 billion in our reconstruction before the deal.

More recently, Roche agreed to acquire Poseida for roughly $1.0 billion upfront equity value and up to $1.5 billion including contingent payments. AstraZeneca acquired Gracell in a transaction worth approximately $1.0 billion upfront and up to $1.2 billion including the contingent component.

AbbVie agreed to pay up to $2.1 billion at closing for Capstan Therapeutics. AstraZeneca paid $425 million upfront for EsoBiotec, with total potential consideration of up to $1 billion. Gilead then completed its acquisition of Arcellx at an implied equity value of about $7.8 billion, with additional contingent consideration possible.

These deals also show how little cumulative funding alone can tell us about eventual strategic value. EsoBiotec sat near the bottom of our funding ranking because relatively little equity financing had been publicly disclosed. Its technology still attracted a potential $1 billion acquisition.

| EsoBiotec | ≥$6M disclosed | AstraZeneca | $425M upfront; up to $1.0B |

## Why can a lightly funded cell therapy startup sell for so much money?

Pharma companies buy differentiated technology and future drug economics, not a reimbursement of the startup's historical fundraising.

EsoBiotec makes the point unusually well. Our public funding reconstruction finds only a small amount of disclosed venture equity compared with the hundreds of millions raised by better-known peers. AstraZeneca nevertheless agreed to pay $425 million upfront and as much as $1 billion in total.

The attraction was an in-vivo platform that could potentially program immune cells through an intravenous infusion and avoid weeks of conventional ex-vivo cell manufacturing.

Arcellx shows the same phenomenon at a much larger scale. Its reconstructed pre-acquisition fundraising of roughly $230 million is tiny compared with the approximately $7.8 billion implied equity value cited by Gilead when it completed the acquisition. The value sat in anito-cel and the underlying binding technology rather than in the amount previously spent financing the company.

The lower half of a funding ranking should not be mistaken for a list of weaker businesses. Capital efficiency, licensing economics and strategic scarcity can create enormous value without producing a giant cumulative fundraising number.

## Which smaller cell therapy startups are attracting attention now?

Some of the most interesting current financings sit well below the billion-dollar leaders because the companies are younger or are pursuing newer approaches.

Umoja stands out with its $100 million Series C for in-vivo CAR-T. AvenCell raised $112 million for switchable CAR-T technology. Aspen secured $115 million for personalized neuron replacement in Parkinson's disease. OriCell raised more than $110 million in its pre-IPO financing while advancing solid-tumor CAR-T programs.

Quell remains a major Treg bet after its $156 million Series B, while Tr1X entered the market with a $75 million Series A for regulatory T-cell therapies.

None of these companies needs to catch Iovance's $3.1 billion lifetime financing total to become important. For younger companies, the more revealing question is how much money investors are willing to commit at the current stage and what milestone that money is supposed to reach.

A $100 million Series B or C today can be more informative about fresh investor conviction than a billion-dollar cumulative total built across 15 years.

## Is cell therapy funding becoming more selective?

Yes. Investors are still writing very large checks, but the recent deals are clustering around a narrower set of technical and clinical ideas.

Recent nine-figure financings include Obsidian in engineered TIL, Immatics in PRAME-directed therapies, Century in iPSC-derived therapies including type 1 diabetes, OriCell in solid-tumor CAR-T and Aspen in neuronal replacement.

At the same time, the historical ranking contains multiple companies that shut down, sold assets, were acquired after financial difficulty or dramatically changed strategy. The market has already absorbed several expensive lessons.

That makes today's environment different from the period when a broad platform story could command a huge private round with very limited human data. Large checks now tend to come with a more concrete thesis: a defined clinical program, an unusual manufacturing advantage, compelling human data, an autoimmune use case or a credible path to a pivotal trial.

The money has not disappeared. It has become harder to earn.

## What does Vor Bio's $1 billion funding history tell us about how fast this market can change?

Vor Bio shows why a cumulative funding ranking can preserve the history of a company even after the company itself has changed direction.

# A Flagship startup secures $121M in new funding

The money will be used to advance its first research programs for metabolic and blood disorders into the clinic, likely within the next two years, the company said.

Published Oct. 4, 2022

Gwendolyn Wu
Senior Reporter

Cellarity, launched in 2017, looks to advance its first research programs in metabolic and blood disorders into the clinic in the next two years.
Permission granted by Cellarity

Cellarity has raised $121 million in its third round of venture financing, bringing the company’s total funding raised since launching in 2017 to $274 million.

The funds will be used to bring Cellarity’s first research programs into clinical testing for metabolic and blood disorders, the biotechnology startup said. 

In recent years, young biotechs often looked to go public after their second, or Series B, round of venture funding. In 2022, however, an increasing number are staying private to avoid the stormy public markets. IPOs have fallen sharply this year among biotech companies, a dropoff that’s been particularly steep for cell and gene therapy startups, according to data from BioPharma Dive.

But Fabrice Chouraqui, Cellarity’s CEO, said the company has “always” eyed a third round of venture investments instead of going public.

“The Series C will allow us to also expand our investor base, which we did with four new investors,” Chouraqui said. “Now looking more into the future, we’re keeping optionality.”

When Flagship Pioneering launched the Somerville, Mass.-based company five years ago, its founders theorized they could create more effective drugs by studying the cellular molecular network — the pathways and relationships between proteins, genes and other parts of the cell. Using artificial intelligence and other technologies, researchers are able to map out each individual cell. That information helps Cellarity develop drug candidates that can target specific cell behavior changes.

“What we are doing is that we are designing drugs to address the underlying cellular dysfunction of the disease,” Chouraqui said.

The company is working on seven research programs targeting metabolic and blood disorders, as well as cancers. Cellarity’s most advanced drug candidates remain preclinical, and are expected to advance to human trials in the next two years, the company said.

“Since the cell is a fuller representation of disease, the platform is uniquely designed to drive higher translatability and clinical success, creating important new medicines for internal pipeline development as well as with partners,” Stephen Berenson, a managing partner at Flagship and chairperson of Cellarity’s board of directors, said in a statement.

Flagship participated in the Series C round, as did four new investors including Tokyo-based Kyowa Kirin Co. and Seoul-based Hanwha Impact Partners.

Previously, the company pulled in $123 million in a Series B round in 2021, and raised $30 million in Series A financing. It has no immediate plans for an IPO or a Series D round, Chouraqui said.

Cellarity is the second Flagship company in two months to raise Series C funding. The other startup that opted for a third private round was Senda Biosciences.

*Correction: A previous version of this story included an incorrect funding total for Cellarity and mischaracterized the company as working in cell and gene therapy.*
